bio.en: Chip Conley is a hospitality entrepreneur (founder of Joie de Vivre Hotels), former strategic advisor to Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky, founder of the Modern Elder Academy, and author on thriving at work as you age.
bio.zh: Chip Conley 是一位酒店业创业者（Joie de Vivre Hotels 创始人）、Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky 的前战略顾问、现代长者学院（Modern Elder Academy）创始人，也是关于“年长者在职场中茁壮成长”的作者。

summary.en: Chip shares what it was like joining Airbnb in his fifties as both mentor and subordinate to Brian Chesky, and why older brains connecting dots alongside fast young teammates is a superpower. He discusses founding the Modern Elder Academy, how a near-death experience changed his life trajectory, and how to build a great culture. The conversation is about success, meaning, and contribution in tech as you age.
summary.zh: Chip 分享了五十多岁加入 Airbnb、既当 Brian Chesky 的导师又当部下的经历，以及为何“年长大脑”与飞速的年轻队友连线是一种超能力。他谈到了创办现代长者学院、一次濒死体验如何改变人生轨迹，以及如何打造优秀文化。对话关于在年岁增长时，于科技行业中获得成功、意义与贡献。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's paint a picture of just what it was like to join Airbnb in your fifties.
turns.zh: 让我们来描绘一下您在 50 岁时加入 Airbnb 的情景。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: I was mentoring Brian, but he was also my boss. I was 52, the average age was 26. I had to be both wise and curious, and often the dumbest person in the room.
turns.zh: 我是布莱恩的导师，但他也是我的老板。我当时 52 岁，平均年龄 26 岁。我必须既聪明又好奇，而且常常是房间里最愚蠢的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's great to be in founder mode. It's not as great to be working for someone in founder mode.
turns.zh: 处于创始人模式真是太好了。为处于创始人模式的人工作并不那么好。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Brian assumed everybody else was going to work at the same pace and duration. His point of view is like, "Hey, we're having a meeting in the office tonight at 10 o'clock. Be there."
turns.zh: 布莱恩认为其他人都会以相同的节奏和持续时间工作。他的观点是，“嘿，我们今晚 10 点在办公室开会。请到场。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyone's talking about, "We got to make the product better. We got to optimize this button, and improve conversion."
turns.zh: 每个人都在谈论，“我们必须让产品变得更好。我们必须优化这个按钮，并提高转化率。”

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Isn't the product the homes and the apartments? Jobot said, "Nope. Product in the tech industry is something different." I just said, "Listen, let's get some older people who are hosts in here."
turns.zh: 产品不就是住宅和公寓吗？乔博特说：“不。科技行业的产品是不同的。”我只是说，“听着，让我们邀请一些老年人来主持吧。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This whole story is a really good example of the value of having folks that are older.
turns.zh: 整个故事是一个很好的例子，说明了拥有年长的人的价值。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: When you have older brains connecting the dots, younger team members being really fast and focused, it's brilliant, and people won't notice your wrinkles as much as they'll notice your energy.
turns.zh: 当你有年长的大脑把各个点联系起来，年轻的团队成员非常快速和专注时，这是很棒的，人们不会像注意到你的能量那样注意到你的皱纹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The Airbnb experienced led you to starting something called the Modern Elder Academy.
turns.zh: Airbnb 的经历让你创办了一个名为“现代老年学院”的机构。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: If you think about the caterpillar to butterfly journey, midlife is the chrysalis. Midlife is not crisis. I'm happier today at 64 than I was at 47 when I was going through my flatline experience.
turns.zh: 如果你想想毛毛虫到蝴蝶的旅程，中年就是蛹。中年不是危机。今天我 64 岁了，比 47 岁时经历平淡经历时更快乐。

What was that like?
turns.zh: 哇，我很荣幸。我很高兴能让你感到骄傲，奇普，相反我也有同样的感觉。我们在 Airbnb 合作多年。我必须向你学习很多东西。我真的很高兴更多的人将从这次对话中向您学习。我认为我们分解这次谈话的方式是将其分为三个部分，这就是你职业生涯的三个弧线。这三个部分分别是你的早期职业生涯、创建 Joie de Vivre、你在 Airbnb 的时光、我们在那里一起工作，然后讨论你现在正在做的事情，即现代老年学院。 (00:05:22)：我其实想从中间的章节开始。我要谈谈我们合作的 Airbnb。让我们来描绘一下你在 50 多岁时加入 Airbnb 的情景，周围都是一群 20 岁、30 岁左右的人，向 Brian Chesky 汇报工作，我不知道他三十多岁了。那是什么样子的？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah, I wasn't planning on doing this. I got a call from a woman named Natalie Tucci who worked at Airbnb, and said, "Brian Chesky and I've been talking about having you come in and give a talk. Are you open to that?" I was like, "Well, what is Airbnb?" This was 13 years ago, I think it was the end of 2012. Then Brian called me and said, "Listen, we really want you to come in." I came in and gave a talk about innovation and hospitality. (00:06:14): I think I didn't realize it was sort of a dress rehearsal for Brian to see whether the younger crowd there, I was 52, the average age was 26, would feel good about an old geezer like me with a bricks and mortar boutique hotel background, talking about the industry that Airbnb was disrupting. As it turns out, people liked me. Brian said, "I want you to come in and work 15 hours a week as a consultant. I want you to be my in-house mentor for both me, and Joe and Nate." I said, "Okay, 15 hours a week is great," and then within three weeks, it was 15 hours a day. (00:07:00): I was saying to Brian, "You're actually not paying me anything." He gave me a little bit of stock that would vest in six months and I said, "I don't know that this deal's working for me. It seems like the company needs to be a little more than you said." He said, "Yeah, I got you. I just wanted you to get in here and see what you could do." Long story short is I ended up going full-time. It was hard at first, Lenny, because I didn't understand the tech lingo. I didn't have any background. I was 52. I'd never worked in a tech company before. (00:07:42): I was mentoring Brian on leadership, but he was also my boss. I was the head of global hospitality and strategy, which meant initially, I was in charge of all the hosts in the world. Over time, that meant a lot more things too. I was involved in many parts of the business, definitely not the technical parts, but I think the hardest thing for me was just that initially, when people were talking about product, and Jobot said, "I'm the chief product officer," and I'm like, "Well, isn't the product the homes and the apartments?" Jobot said, "No, product in the tech industry is something different." (00:08:23): I had to be both wise and curious, and often the dumbest person in the room. It required me to have a certain amount of humility as well as to be reporting to a guy 21 years younger than me, Brian.
turns.zh: 是的，我本来没打算这么做。我接到一位在 Airbnb 工作、名叫娜塔莉·图奇 (Natalie Tucci) 的女士打来的电话，她说：“布莱恩·切斯基 (Brian Chesky) 和我一直在讨论让你进来演讲。你愿意吗？”我当时想，“那么，Airbnb 是什么？”那是 13 年前的事了，我想那是 2012 年底。然后布莱恩打电话给我说：“听着，我们真的希望你加入。”我进来做了一个关于创新和热情好客的演讲。 (00:06:14)：我想我没有意识到这是 Brian 的一次彩排，目的是看看那里的年轻人群（我今年 52 岁，平均年龄为 26 岁）是否会对像我这样有实体精品酒店背景的老家伙谈论 Airbnb 正在颠覆的行业感觉良好。事实证明，人们喜欢我。布莱恩说：“我希望你作为顾问每周工作 15 个小时。我希望你成为我、乔和内特的内部导师。”我说，“好吧，每周工作 15 小时就很好了”，然后三周之内，就变成了每天 15 小时。 (00:07:00)：我对布莱恩说，“你实际上没有付给我任何东西。”他给了我一点股票，六个月后归属，我说，“我不知道这笔交易对我有用。看来公司需要比你说的多一点。”他说：“是的，我找到你了。我只是想让你进来看看你能做什么。”长话短说，我最终成为了全职员工。莱尼，一开始很难，因为我不懂技术术语。我没有任何背景。我当时 52 岁。我以前从未在科技公司工作过。 (00:07:42)：我在领导力方面指导布莱恩，但他也是我的老板。我是全球酒店和战略主管，这意味着最初我负责世界上所有的东道主。随着时间的推移，这也意味着更多的事情。我参与了业务的许多部分，绝对不是技术部分，但我认为对我来说最困难的事情就是最初，当人们谈论产品时，Jobot 说，“我是首席产品官”，我想，“好吧，产品不就是住宅和公寓吗？”乔博特说：“不，科技行业的产品是不同的。” (00:08:23)：我必须既聪明又好奇，而且常常是房间里最愚蠢的人。这要求我有一定的谦逊，并且要向比我小 21 岁的布莱恩汇报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That actually, the point you're making there about what is the product I asked Laura Hughes, formerly Laura Modi, what to talk to you about, who we got to work together. She's the CEO of Bobbie now. You worked closely with her at Airbnb. She said this was the thing that stuck with her most about working with you is coming in and everyone's talking about, "We got to make the product better. We got to optimize this button and improve conversion, and product, product, product." (00:08:59): You're just like, "What is the product? I thought the product of Airbnb was the hosts, and the experiences, and the trips." I think that shows the value of someone like you coming in with different experience, and also older, and helping us communicate differently to hosts who also don't understand.
turns.zh: 事实上，你在那里提出的关于产品是什么的观点，我问劳拉·休斯（Laura Hughes），原名劳拉·莫迪（Laura Modi），要和你谈谈什么，我们要和谁一起工作。她现在是Bobbie的首席执行官。您在 Airbnb 与她密切合作。她说，这是与您合作时最困扰她的事情，每个人都在谈论，“我们必须让产品变得更好。我们必须优化这个按钮并提高转化率，以及产品、产品、产品。” (00:08:59)：你会想，“产品是什么？我认为 Airbnb 的产品是房东、体验和旅行。”我认为这显示了像您这样拥有不同经验且年长的人的价值，帮助我们以不同的方式与同样不理解的房东进行沟通。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Well, there's an interesting thing also, Lenny, and you notice the difference in age between our hosts and our guests was probably about 10 years maybe. Over time, it actually got higher, because we started actually reaching out more aggressively to boomers and Gen Xers to be hosts. You had, I remember at one point, and again, let's get into a product talk here, I remember at one point, there was a conversation that was going on about taking Airbnb so it was mobile only. (00:09:47): Partly because back in the day, the two sharing economy darlings were Uber and Airbnb. Of course, Uber was pretty much a mobile only app. Airbnb started as non-mobile and then went mobile. Then it was like, "Oh, wouldn't it be interesting if everything was mobile?" At some point, I just said, "Listen, let's get some older people who are hosts in here to see how well they will be versed in managing their listing purely on mobile." (00:10:18): There were times where I was a voice for older users, in this case, hosts, that was helpful to guys and women in their twenties who were the engineers and designers and product managers. I always liked working with you. I want to just compliment Lenny for a minute.
turns.zh: 嗯，还有一件有趣的事情，莱尼，你注意到我们的主人和客人之间的年龄差异可能大约有 10 岁。随着时间的推移，它实际上变得更高，因为我们实际上开始更积极地接触婴儿潮一代和 X 世代作为东道主。我记得有一次，我们再次在这里进行产品讨论，我记得有一次，正在进行一场关于采用 Airbnb 的对话，因此它只能是移动的。 (00:09:47)：部分原因是在当时，共享经济的两个宠儿是 Uber 和 Airbnb。当然，Uber 基本上是一款移动应用程序。 Airbnb 最初是非移动业务，后来转向移动业务。然后就想，“哦，如果一切都是移动的，那不是很有趣吗？”在某个时候，我只是说，“听着，让我们找一些年纪较大的房东来看看他们在移动设备上管理房源的熟练程度。” (00:10:18)：有时我为老年用户（在本例中为主持人）代言，这对二十多岁的工程师、设计师和产品经理很有帮助。我一直很喜欢和你一起工作。我只想赞美莱尼一分钟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, how sweet is that?
turns.zh: 哦，那有多甜蜜？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: We did a lot of different things together, and what I appreciated was you had a humility to you that was different than a lot of the other product managers. There's other product managers, I'm not going to mention their names, and some of these product managers were very good. There were other product managers though who I found it sometimes hard to work with, because they expected me to know as much as they did. (00:11:07): I guess it would be, if the opposite side of that would be an older manager expecting a younger manager to have as much emotional intelligence, because emotional intelligence on average is something we get better at as we get older. I think the key for me to work in that environment and make it work was to not pretend to know things I didn't know, it was to have a sense of humor and humility in how I operated, and it was to show respect and hope that I got it in return. I don't know if you felt that way, Lenny. That's the kind of environment I tried to embody there.
turns.zh: 我们一起做了很多不同的事情，我欣赏的是你的谦逊，这与许多其他产品经理不同。还有其他的产品经理，我就不提他们的名字了，其中有一些产品经理非常优秀。但我发现有时很难与其他产品经理一起工作，因为他们希望我知道的和他们一样多。 (00:11:07)：我想，如果相反的一面是年长的经理期望年轻的经理有同样多的情商，因为平均情商是我们随着年龄的增长而变得更好的东西。我认为我在那种环境中工作并使其发挥作用的关键是不要假装知道我不知道的事情，而是在我的运作方式中保持幽默感和谦虚感，并且表现出尊重并希望我得到回报。我不知道你是否也有这样的感觉，莱尼。这就是我试图在那里体现的那种环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. There's a couple of threads there I want to follow. One is just working for Brian. A lot of people talk about founder mode, and the power of founder mode, it's so great. That's how we-
turns.zh: 绝对地。我想关注几个线程。其中一个只是为布莱恩工作。很多人都在讲创始人模式，创始人模式的威力，实在是太强大了。我们就是这样——

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Guess who-
turns.zh: 猜猜是谁——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: ... populated that recently, that was Brian.
turns.zh: ...最近出现的那个人就是布莱恩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly. It's great to be in founder mode. It's not as great to be working for someone in founder mode. Often a very challenging place to be.
turns.zh: 确切地。处于创始人模式真是太好了。为处于创始人模式的人工作并不那么好。通常是一个非常具有挑战性的地方。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You reported to Brian. Also, you were just your own boss basically your entire career. You never really had to report to someone before. Also, he was in his thirties, you're in your fifties. What was it like working for Brian? The more real you can be, the better, because a lot of people always talk about here, it's like, "It was wonderful, I learned so much." Just like what was that experience? What did you learn from working for someone like Brian?
turns.zh: 你向布莱恩汇报了。而且，基本上你的整个职业生涯都是你自己的老板。以前你从来不需要向别人汇报。而且，他三十多岁了，你五十多岁了。为布莱恩工作感觉如何？你越真实越好，因为很多人总是在这里谈论，就像，“这太棒了，我学到了很多东西。”就像那次经历是什么？你从为布莱恩这样的人工作中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Well, let's start with the fact that I would never have gone to work for Airbnb if I didn't believe in Brian, because quite frankly, when Brian approached me and we started talking about it, I was like, I wasn't sure I liked the business model all that well as a hotelier. I had to believe in something beyond the business model, because I wasn't sure that the business model would work. Although soon after joining, I saw the numbers. I was like, "Wow, this is working pretty well." (00:12:56): I believed in Brian because the thing that Brian showed up with initially was just a curiosity and an appetite for learning. I remember back in 2011, when the big debacle happened with the apartment getting trashed by a guest. Brian decided he was going to go to find George Tenet, the former head of the CIA. Brian would go to experts and say to the expert, "I don't know what the hell I'm doing." He did that with me when it came to hospitality. I appreciated that a guy who had a lot of hubris, and Brian definitely has a lot of hubris, could also have the humility to say, "I want to learn more about this." (00:13:42): It's sort of a growth mindset. What was hard with Brian is, I'd say, three things. Number one is Brian assumed everybody else was going to work at the same pace and duration, and he still has this issue. The beautiful thing about Brian is he's been very honest in the last couple of years on podcasts about his workaholism, and about the fact that the way he lives his life is not like other people. Back when I joined, his point of view is like, "Hey, we're having a meeting in the office tonight at 10 o'clock, be there." (00:14:20): It's like, "Really? No, I don't think so." I think the fact that Brian assumed everybody else was as one-dimensional in their focus as him was at times a problem, especially for a guy like me who was, I was in a stage in my career where I have a lot of interests. That was one. Number two is Brian admires and admired back then, Steve Jobs so much that there was a sense that as a guy who came from the product world, from the Rhode Island School of Design, he knew better than anybody else. (00:15:05): There was this, one of the challenges for a CEO sometimes, and this was my experience in my 24 years of running Joie de Vivre, my boutique hotel company, is it feels good when you feel needed. To come into a room and sort of see something, and then point out the things that are wrong makes you feel good. If you don't have emotional intelligence, that process can really piss people off or demotivate people. In Brian's case, I didn't have to deal with that too much, because he didn't understand, when I was starting, it was really, I was in charge of the hosts around the world. (00:15:45): Quite frankly, the idea of what's the psychology of the host? What's a host entrepreneur like? I went on a world tour to 20 different cities, and went and talked to hosts. I think I came back from that with a little bit of credibility with Brian to say like, "Hey, yes, our data science team and the quality folks who are doing qualitative interviews, they're getting something out of this." I actually went into the homes of these hosts all around the world, and I think I was lucky because Brian did less of that than he did with other people. (00:16:19): For the product team, my God, a product meeting with Brian would keep people up the night before, not just because they were actually working all night long to get prepared, but also they knew they would work all night long, because they probably wouldn't sleep in anticipation for this. That was another issue, I'd say. I'd say the other thing that, and in each of these cases, I think Brian's getting better. Just like Steve Jobs got better over time when he left and then he came back, he was much better when he came back, from all the people I've talked with who worked with him. (00:16:53): I'd say the third thing for Brian was the sense that adding a zero to something in terms of expectations, or thinking you're going to set a deadline that is unreasonable is necessary. If you don't do that, there's almost an underlying message that people won't kick ass on their own. There was a sense that Brian had that he had to maybe create ridiculous goals, because even if we hit half of that goal, it was very encouraging. What he missed in that was the fact that when you miss a goal, and when you have someone who has power over you setting the goal, or encouraging a particular goal, you're setting people up for a lot of stress. (00:17:51): At the end of the day, I think Brian is a generational leader as a millennial, and I think he deserves a lot of credit. Airbnb is as successful as it is, partly because of Brian's leadership. I would not have been there without him. Having said that, I had to hold my tongue in meetings sometimes when I saw how he was operating, because I wouldn't have done it that way. I think over time, I hope I had a little bit of influence on him in terms of how to apply some emotional intelligence to leading people.
turns.zh: 好吧，让我们从这样一个事实开始：如果我不相信 Brian，我永远不会去 Airbnb 工作，因为坦率地说，当 Brian 接近我并我们开始谈论它时，我当时想，我不确定我是否喜欢酒店经营者的商业模式。我必须相信商业模式之外的东西，因为我不确定商业模式是否有效。尽管加入后不久，我就看到了这些数字。我当时想，“哇，这工作得很好。” (00:12:56)：我相信布莱恩，因为布莱恩最初表现出来的只是好奇心和学习欲望。我记得 2011 年，公寓被一位客人乱扔垃圾，发生了一场大灾难。布莱恩决定去找前中央情报局局长乔治·特尼特。布莱恩会去找专家并对专家说：“我不知道我到底在做什么。”当谈到热情好客时，他对我也是这样做的。我很欣赏一个非常傲慢的人，布莱恩肯定也非常傲慢，也可以谦虚地说：“我想了解更多这方面的知识。” (00:13:42)：这是一种成长心态。我想说，布莱恩的困难在于三件事。第一，布莱恩认为其他人都会以相同的速度和持续时间工作，但他仍然有这个问题。布莱恩的美妙之处在于，过去几年他在播客上非常诚实地谈论了他的工作狂，以及他的生活方式与其他人不同的事实。当我加入时，他的观点是，“嘿，我们今晚 10 点在办公室开会，请到场。” (00:14:20)：就像是，“真的吗？不，我不这么认为。”我认为布莱恩认为其他人的注意力都像他一样是一维的，这一事实有时是一个问题，特别是对于像我这样的人来说，我正处于职业生涯的一个阶段，我有很多兴趣。那是一个。第二个是布赖恩当时非常钦佩和钦佩史蒂夫·乔布斯，以至于有一种感觉，作为一个来自产品世界、来自罗德岛设计学院的人，他比任何人都了解。 (00:15:05)：有时，CEO 面临的挑战之一是，这是我在经营 Joie de Vivre（我的精品酒店公司）24 年来的经验，那就是，当你感到被需要时，感觉会很好。走进一个房间，看到一些东西，然后指出错误的地方，会让你感觉很好。如果你没有情商，这个过程真的会让人生气或失去积极性。就布莱恩而言，我不必处理太多问题，因为他不明白，当我开始时，我真的负责世界各地的东道主。 (00:15:45): 坦白说，主持人的心理是什么？主持人企业家是什么样的？我进行了一次世界巡演，去了 20 个不同的城市，并去和主持人交谈。我想我从布莱恩那里得到了一点可信度，我说：“嘿，是的，我们的数据科学团队和正在进行定性访谈的高质量人员，他们正在从中得到一些东西。”事实上，我走进了世界各地这些主人的家中，我认为我很幸运，因为布莱恩做的事情比他对其他人所做的要少。 (00:16:19)：对于产品团队来说，天哪，与 Brian 的产品会议会让人们在前一天晚上彻夜难眠，不仅因为他们实际上整夜工作以做好准备，而且他们知道自己会整夜工作，因为他们可能不会为此而睡觉。我想说，那是另一个问题。我想说的是，在每一种情况下，我认为布莱恩都在变得更好。就像史蒂夫·乔布斯随着时间的推移，他离开然后回来时变得更好一样，从所有与我交谈过的与他共事的人来看，他回来后也变得更好了。 (00:16:53)：我想说布莱恩的第三件事是在期望方面加零，或者认为你要设定不合理的最后期限是必要的。如果你不这样做，几乎就会传达出一个潜在的信息：人们不会自己踢屁股。布莱恩有一种感觉，他可能必须制定一些荒谬的目标，因为即使我们实现了目标的一半，这也是非常令人鼓舞的。他忽略了这样一个事实：当你错过一个目标时，当你有一个对你有权力的人设定目标或鼓励一个特定的目标时，你就会给人们带来很大的压力。 (00:17:51)：归根结底，我认为布莱恩是千禧一代的一代领袖，我认为他值得很多赞誉。 Airbnb 如此成功，部分原因在于布莱恩的领导力。没有他我就不会在那里。话虽如此，有时当我看到他的运作方式时，我不得不在会议上保持沉默，因为我不会那样做。我想随着时间的推移，我希望我在如何运用一些情商来领导别人方面对他产生一点影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For people in this position, a lot of people work for founders, especially now that founder mode is a thing. Every founder is just like, "I'm the founder, you got to do what I tell you. It's founder mode. Again, this is how we win. We're in founder mode." You shared really good insight of building credibility as a really good lever to work better with someone like that. Is there anything else you just think as tactics to be effective with founders in founder mode?
turns.zh: 对于这个职位的人来说，很多人都在为创始人工作，尤其是现在创始人模式已经流行起来。每个创始人都会说，“我是创始人，你必须按照我告诉你的去做。这是创始人模式。再说一次，这就是我们获胜的方式。我们处于创始人模式。”您分享了关于建立信誉的非常好的见解，这是与这样的人更好地合作的一个很好的杠杆。您认为还有什么其他策略可以在创始人模式下有效地对待创始人吗？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Knowing what I know now, I would say, "Lenny, let's do a little pep talk, you and me before the meeting." I want you to start the meeting with the following as you present and Brian's in the room. "Brian, let's talk about what we're trying to accomplish here. Let's get really clear," and you probably did this, but, "let's get really clear on what both, what's the intention of this iteration that we're doing on the product? What defines success, and what do I want to get accomplished in this meeting?" (00:19:25): You start with that, because that actually helps to make sure there's alignment. Frankly, if there's not alignment, you might as well not have the meeting. Let's spend the rest of this meeting talking about alignment. That's what I would do, because that's something you can come back to over and over again during the rest of the meeting when Brian or the founder, whomever it is, is beating you up on something, saying like, "Well, let me tell you why it looks like that or why we're doing that." It goes back to that, the three principles or the three key goals we're trying to do with this product update. Yeah, so try to set alignment on the front end.
turns.zh: 知道我现在所知道的情况后，我会说：“莱尼，让我们在会议前，你和我做一些鼓舞人心的演讲。”我希望您在布赖恩在场时进行以下发言，以开始会议。 “Brian，让我们谈谈我们想要在这里实现的目标。让我们真正弄清楚，”您可能会这样做，但是，“让我们真正弄清楚这两者是什么，我们在产品上所做的这次迭代的目的是什么？成功的定义是什么，我想在这次会议中完成什么？” (00:19:25)：你从这个开始，因为这实际上有助于确保一致性。坦率地说，如果不一致，你还不如不参加会议。让我们在本次会议的剩余时间里讨论协调问题。这就是我会做的，因为在会议的剩余时间里，当布莱恩或创始人，无论是谁，在某件事上殴打你时，你可以一遍又一遍地回顾这一点，比如，“好吧，让我告诉你为什么它看起来像那样，或者我们为什么这样做。”这又回到了我们试图通过此产品更新实现的三个原则或三个关键目标。是的，所以尝试在前端设置对齐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an important tip for anyone working with anyone, even. I love just that that works especially well here. Then just going back to the credibility piece, what you shared there is you went on this world tour, not something everyone can do, but just getting really close to your customers, and using that as a, "Hey, I actually know what I'm talking about. You actually should listen to me even though you're the founder."
turns.zh: 对于任何与任何人一起工作的人来说，这都是一个重要的提示。我喜欢它在这里特别有效。然后回到可信度部分，你在那里分享的是你参加了这次世界巡演，不是每个人都能做的事情，而是真正接近你的客户，并将其用作“嘿，我实际上知道我在说什么。即使你是创始人，你实际上也应该听我的。”

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah, I think the other thing is PowerPoint or whatever tool you're using, just be careful about being overly reliant upon it, especially when you have a combustible founder who may take you off path, such that your deck in its current order makes no sense at all. I always wanted to really limit the deck as much as possible, because I didn't know where the meeting was going to go. I wanted the decks helpful at the start, at the very start, to just set principles, set goals. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为另一件事是 PowerPoint 或你正在使用的任何工具，只是要小心不要过度依赖它，尤其是当你有一个易怒的创始人，他可能会让你偏离正轨，这样你的套牌按照当前的顺序就毫无意义了。我一直想尽可能地限制牌组，因为我不知道会议要去哪里。我希望这些套牌从一开始就能够帮助我们设定原则、设定目标。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This whole story of you joining Airbnb in your fifties is a really good example of intergenerational collaboration, something that you're big on, just the value of having folks that are older working at tech companies. Maybe just talk about that broadly, and then we segue into other elements of your career.
turns.zh: 您在 50 多岁时加入 Airbnb 的整个故事是代际合作的一个很好的例子，这是您所热衷的事情，也是让年长的人在科技公司工作的价值所在。也许只是广泛地谈论这一点，然后我们继续讨论你职业生涯的其他要素。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: I wrote a book called Wisdom at Work: the Making of a Modern Elder after my Airbnb experience. I did a lot of research. I was like, "Wow, so why do we have less intergenerational collaboration in the workplace, especially in Silicon Valley than we could use?" I started interviewing people, then I started talking to brain scientists, neuroscientists, and realized that a younger brain has fluid intelligence, tends to be fast and focused, really good at problem solving, very good at linearity in terms of looking at things. (00:21:59): As you get older, the brain shrinks a little bit and you have crystallized intelligence. In crystallized intelligence, what's going on is you're going from left brain to right brain more adeptly. There's a little bit less focus, a little more holistic thinking, systemic thinking, connecting the dots. You can imagine that on a team when you have older brains connecting the dots, thinking broadly, peripherally, younger team members being really fast and focused, and being able to think linearly how to get things done, that combination can either be successful or not. (00:22:36): When it's successful. It's brilliant. I think Laura, Laura Modi, Laura Hughes Modi, who was my director of hospitality, but also we worked in so many different capacities with her in the company, I loved working with her because her brain worked different than my brain. That's the opportunity is when you realize that diversity on a team, there's lots of kinds of diversity, but when it comes to brain diversity, not just with neuro diverse people but age diverse people, you get a benefit, an effective benefit that is not as noticeable, quite frankly, in some other diversities. (00:23:16): I found that over and over was really helpful. Part of my job sometimes was to find the blind spot. Again, if you are very focused, one of the things I said to Brian early on was, "I've seen the business plan. Now, I know the goals of how big we want to be in three years." This was very early in my tenure. I said, "But what we really have done, everything we're trying to do is to have no regulations and pay no occupancy tax." Now, hotels pay a bed tax, occupancy tax, we're not paying it, and we're trying to do everything we can not to pay it. (00:23:51): Knowing that, so for our listeners and viewers to know this, this is something that a guest pays. It's not the host who pays it, the guest pays it. It's part of the bill. If you go and stay in a hotel, there's a big, big tax part of the bill, but it made us more affordable by not having to have our guests pay taxes. Long story short is I said to Brian, "If we're as big as we're going to be three years from now, I promise you we're going to be regulated. I promise you we're going to be paying occupancy taxes. Let's take some proactive steps toward building a strategy for how we're going to be regulated." (00:24:28): That has consistently been Airbnb's biggest challenge is regulation in municipal markets all around the world. If we'd started a little earlier, maybe in New York, maybe in New York, it wouldn't have gotten to the point where it has been toxic in New York for the last dozen years ever since I was there. There's a few other markets in the world where it was like that. I would just say the value in having some age diversity, even when you have an older person reporting to a younger person, is it can be collaborative. (00:25:02): There was a guy named John Q. Smith, an engineer who I think you probably remember him at Airbnb. This is a guy who looked younger than he was, and he was a little bit nervous about telling people his age. The thing that was great about John is over time, he was not necessarily going to be the best coder at Airbnb. There was a whole new collection of coders coming in every month, but he became a great manager. (00:25:32): The beautiful thing about moving from the individual contributor to the manager, the person who can actually bring out the best in a bunch of younger people, who may be better technically than he or she is, but they know how to elevate talent. I call this invisible productivity. It's productivity in which you make everybody else around you better. That's something I tried to do with my teams at Airbnb. Ultimately, I had six different teams, five hospitality and five other teams reporting to me. I did my best to just be the kind of person who wasn't solving all the problems, but I was trying to elevate. (00:26:11): There's a woman named Lisa Dubost who is at Airbnb, and she, one day, the HR department was reporting to me at one point, and she was running HR. She was 25 and had no background in HR at all. One day she came in to me and she just said, "Chip, you are my confidant." Lisa has a French accent and fluent in French. She said confidant in just the right way. I said, "Oh, well thank you, Lisa." I said to her, "You haven't given me any juicy details yet. A confidant is someone who has the secrets." (00:26:42): She said to me, "No, in my part of France, a confidant is somebody who gives you confidence." It was like, "Oh, well, maybe that's what a mentor can be is a confidant, someone who gives you confidence and helps by asking questions, helps you as the younger mentee find your roadmap to success."
turns.zh: 在 Airbnb 的经历之后，我写了一本名为《工作中的智慧：现代长者的塑造》的书。我做了很多研究。我当时想，“哇，那么为什么我们在工作场所，尤其是在硅谷，代际合作比我们可以利用的要少呢？”我开始采访人们，然后开始与脑科学家、神经科学家交谈，并意识到年轻的大脑具有流体智力，往往速度快且专注，非常擅长解决问题，非常擅长看待事物的线性。 (00:21:59)：随着年龄的增长，大脑会稍微萎缩，智力就会结晶。在结晶智力中，发生的事情是你更熟练地从左脑转移到右脑。焦点少一点，多一点整体思考、系统思考，将各个点联系起来。你可以想象，在一个团队中，如果年长的大脑能够将各个点联系起来，进行广泛、外围的思考，而年轻的团队成员非常快速且专注，并且能够线性思考如何完成工作，那么这种组合要么成功，要么失败。 (00:22:36)：当成功时。太棒了。我想劳拉、劳拉·莫迪、劳拉·休斯·莫迪，她是我的接待总监，而且我们在公司里与她一起担任过很多不同的职务，我喜欢和她一起工作，因为她的大脑与我的大脑工作方式不同。这就是机会，当你意识到团队的多样性时，有很多种多样性，但当涉及到大脑多样性时，不仅是神经多样化的人，而且是年龄多样化的人，你会得到一个好处，一种有效的好处，坦率地说，在其他一些多样性中并不那么明显。 (00:23:16)：我发现一遍又一遍确实很有帮助。有时我工作的一部分就是找到盲点。再说一次，如果你非常专注，我早些时候对布莱恩说的一件事是，“我已经看过商业计划。现在，我知道我们在三年内想要达到多大的目标。”这是我任期的早期。我说：“但我们真正所做的是，我们所做的一切都是没有法规，也不缴纳占用税。”现在，酒店要缴纳床位税、占用税，我们不缴纳，而且我们正在尽一切努力不缴纳。 (00:23:51)：知道这一点，让我们的听众和观众知道这一点，这是客人付费的。不是主人付钱，而是客人付钱。这是账单的一部分。如果你去住一家酒店，帐单中会有很大一部分税费，但由于不必让我们的客人缴税，这使我们更加负担得起。长话短说，我对布莱恩说：“如果我们三年后发展到现在的规模，我向你保证，我们将受到监管。我向你保证，我们将缴纳占用税。让我们采取一些积极主动的措施，制定如何受到监管的战略。” (00:24:28)：全球市政市场的监管一直是 Airbnb 面临的最大挑战。如果我们早一点开始，也许在纽约，也许在纽约，就不会发展到自从我在那里以来的过去十几年里纽约一直有毒的地步。世界上还有一些其他市场也是如此。我只想说，年龄多样性的价值在于，即使你有一个年长的人向一个年轻人汇报，它也可以是协作的。 (00:25:02)：有一位名叫 John Q. Smith 的工程师，我想您可能还记得 Airbnb 的他。这是一个看上去比实际年龄还要年轻的家伙，对于告诉别人自己的年龄他还有点紧张。 John 的伟大之处在于，随着时间的推移，他不一定会成为 Airbnb 最好的程序员。每个月都有一批新的程序员加入，但他成为了一名出色的经理。 (00:25:32)：从个人贡献者转变为经理的美妙之处在于，经理实际上可以激发一群年轻人的最佳能力，他们在技术上可能比他或她更好，但他们知道如何提升人才。我称之为隐形生产力。生产力是你让周围的人变得更好的生产力。这是我和 Airbnb 团队尝试做的事情。最终，我有六个不同的团队，五个接待团队和五个其他团队向我汇报。我尽力成为那种不能解决所有问题的人，但我正在努力提升。 (00:26:11)：Airbnb 上有一位名叫丽莎·杜博斯特 (Lisa Dubost) 的女士，有一天，她在人力资源部门向我汇报，她负责人力资源部门的工作。她25岁，完全没有人力资源背景。有一天，她来找我，只是说：“奇普，你是我的知己。”丽莎有法国口音，法语流利。她用正确的方式说知己。我说：“噢，谢​​谢你，丽莎。”我对她说：“你还没有告诉我任何有趣的细节。知己就是拥有秘密的人。” (00:26:42)：她对我说：“不，在我所在的法国，知己是给你信心的人。”就像，“哦，好吧，也许这就是导师可以做的就是一个知己，一个给你信心并通过提问来帮助你的人，帮助你作为年轻的受训者找到成功的路线图。”

turns.zh: 您分享了很多很好的例子，说明了老年人在科技公司工作的价值。让我问你，科技领域的年龄歧视有多真实？我问这个问题是因为很多正在招聘的人可能会想，不，不，我没有偏见。我要雇用最好的人。如果他们是五十多岁的人，我就会雇用他们。没问题。感觉实际情况并不经常如此。这个问题到底有多真实？你看到了什么？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah, it's clearly a problem. I'd say it's maybe a little bit less of a problem than it was a dozen years ago, because I think a dozen years ago, it was almost a blind spot. In Airbnb, we had a group called Wisdom at Airbnb. It was an employee resource group for people 40 and older. There are lots of these kinds of groups that didn't exist a dozen years ago in all kinds of tech companies, which is good, because it means that there's a voice and a way to congregate with a bunch of people who are older. (00:28:00): Ultimately, we had these senior nomads come in and be like the voice of the customer for 10 weeks at Airbnb. It was the Wisdom at Airbnb older employee group that really actually pushed for this with Brian. The challenge is, in a world in which the smartest new people, especially when it comes to technical skills and engineering, are coming in with a whole new set of skills that an older person doesn't have, the older person is both expensive and may be perceived as slow. In the era of AI, it's a whole new ballgame. (00:28:42): The question, I think, will be if what AI cannot do is the human wisdom piece, artificial intelligence and human wisdom might be the balance beams here. Is it possible that older managers who have a little more emotional intelligence, a little more pattern recognition, a little bit more wisdom, can be a value to a company? The jury's still out. There's a New York Times article that just came out about the question of is AI going to wipe out older people's jobs or younger people's jobs? I think the answer is both, but the question is how bad is it for both of them? (00:29:29): I think what I would say to an older person, and when I say older, I mean like 45 or older, if you've done well financially and you're doing okay, the question you might ask yourself is, are you open, as I ultimately was with Brian in my fourth year at Airbnb? I took a substantial pay cut. I think it went down to 40% or 50% time, and my stock, my options were dropped to that level, my salaries dropped to that level, because I didn't want to work full time anymore. There are a lot of people who can be valuable in a company who have some institutional wisdom, some process knowledge of how to get things done in this organization. (00:30:08): In tech companies, that's really important. Airbnb, one of the biggest challenges that Airbnb has always been, how do I get shit done around here? Process knowledge allows you to understand, how do you deal with an org chart and get things done partly because you understand the motivations of different groups? That is something you build over time. Long story short is I just think that older people might look at their workload and say, "I'm willing to take a 20% or a 40% pay cut to go to 80% or 60% time," and the company is going to get their money's worth in that.
turns.zh: 是的，这显然是一个问题。我想说，与十几年前相比，这可能不是一个问题，因为我认为十几年前，这几乎是一个盲点。在 Airbnb，我们有一个名为 Wisdom at Airbnb 的小组。这是一个针对 40 岁及以上人士的员工资源小组。在各种科技公司中，有很多十几年前不存在的此类群体，这很好，因为这意味着有一个声音和一种方式可以与一群年长的人聚集在一起。 (00:28:00)：最终，我们让这些高级游牧者加入进来，在 Airbnb 工作了 10 周，为客户代言。真正与 Brian 共同推动这一举措的是 Airbnb 老员工团体的 Wisdom。面临的挑战是，在这个世界上，最聪明的新人，尤其是在技术技能和工程方面，正在拥有老年人不具备的一套全新技能，老年人既昂贵又可能被认为是缓慢的。在人工智能时代，这是一个全新的游戏。 (00:28:42)：我认为，问题是人工智能不能做的事情是人类智慧的一部分，人工智能和人类智慧可能是这里的平衡木。情商多一点、模式识别多一点、智慧多一点的老管理者是否有可能对公司产生价值？陪审团还没有定论。 《纽约时报》刚刚发表了一篇文章，讨论人工智能会取代老年人的工作还是年轻人的工作？我认为答案是两者都是，但问题是这对他们俩来说有多糟糕？ (00:29:29)：我想我会对年长的人说些什么，当我说年长时，我的意思是 45 岁或以上，如果你经济状况良好并且过得还不错，你可能会问自己的问题是，你是否持开放态度，就像我在 Airbnb 的第四年和 Brian 一样？我大幅减薪。我认为它下降到了 40% 或 50% 的时间，我的股票、我的期权都下降到了这个水平，我的工资也下降到了那个水平，因为我不想再全职工作了。有很多人在公司中很有价值，他们拥有一些制度智慧，一些关于如何在组织中完成工作的流程知识。 (00:30:08)：在科技公司中，这非常重要。 Airbnb，Airbnb 一直面临的最大挑战之一，我如何在这里完成任务？流程知识可以让您了解如何处理组织结构图并完成工作，部分原因是您了解不同群体的动机？这是你随着时间的推移而建立的。长话短说，我只是认为老年人可能会考虑他们的工作量并说，“我愿意减薪 20% 或 40%，以达到 80% 或 60% 的工作时间”，而公司将在这方面让他们的钱物有所值。

turns.zh: 这是一个非常有趣的观点，如果你年纪大了，你可能不太了解最前沿的构建和编码方式，人工智能在很多方面会让你变得更容易，你开始只需要与它交谈。您甚至不需要了解下面发生的事情。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: I think this idea being a mentor and a mentor and an intern, there's just the voracious appetite for curiosity. When I talk to someone who's a midlife and wants to be in the tech world or already is, the thing I say is, "Show up with curiosity and a passionate engagement for what you do, and people won't necessarily notice your wrinkles as much as they'll notice your energy." Energy has two parts to it. Energy is, they notice that you are not just sort of resting on your laurels, you have physical energy in how you do your job. (00:32:04): When people are like that, they're sort of timeless. They're age fluid, as I say. We talk about gender fluidity. Well, there could be age fluidity. They're not defined by their age. The other part of energy that's important is being positive. That's sort of more energetic, a little bit more California energetic. There's a sense of when someone's got good energy, you're drawn to them. It's about showing up with the kind of energy of someone 10 or 20 years younger than you, and then showing up with positive energy. (00:32:38): I think one of the things that would say I did well at, there's lots of things I didn't do well at Airbnb, but in terms of what I did well is I was very approachable. Over the course of time, the number of mentees I had, the number of people who just wanted to have coffee with me or tea, the number of people who just said, "Thank you for being in that meeting, you just sort of gave it a positive feeling," was really important. (00:33:04): My energy, both the positive energy part, and then also the fact that yeah, I could work 60 and 70 hours a week, and I could travel around the world as the Secretary of State of the company, which is what Brian called me a couple times on stage. The fact that I could do that meant that no one was looking at me and saying, "Let's get rid of the old fogey." Well, maybe some people the board, but I wasn't aware of them. I just think show up with that passionate engagement, that curiosity, that energy, the ability to be both the learner and the teacher, with respect for people that are younger than you, and you're going to probably do pretty well.
turns.zh: 我认为作为导师、导师和实习生的这个想法，就是对好奇心的贪婪胃口。当我和一个人到中年、想要进入科技界或已经进入科技界时，我会说：“带着好奇心和对你所做的事情的热情投入，人们不一定会注意到你的皱纹，而是会注意到你的精力。”能量有两个部分。能量是，他们注意到你不只是安于现状，你在工作中拥有体力。 (00:32:04)：当人们像那样时，他们就有点永恒了。正如我所说，它们是年龄流体。我们谈论性别流动性。嗯，可能存在年龄流动性。他们不是由年龄来定义的。能量的另一重要部分是积极的。这有点更有活力，更有加州的活力。有一种感觉，当某人精力充沛时，你就会被他们吸引。就是带着比你小10岁、20岁的人的能量出现，然后带着正能量出现。 (00:32:38)：我认为我做得很好的一件事是，我在 Airbnb 有很多事情做得不好，但就我做得好的方面来说，我非常平易近人。随着时间的推移，我有多少学员，有多少人只是想和我一起喝咖啡或茶，有多少人只是说，“谢谢你参加那次会议，你只是给了它一种积极的感觉”，这些都非常重要。 (00:33:04)：我的能量，既是正能量的部分，也是事实，是的，我可以每周工作 60 到 70 小时，而且我可以作为公司的国务卿环游世界，布莱恩在舞台上几次这样称呼我。事实上，我能做到这一点，这意味着没有人看着我说：“让我们摆脱这个老家伙吧。”好吧，也许有些人是董事会成员，但我不知道他们。我只是认为，只要表现出热情、好奇心、活力、既是学习者又是老师的能力，尊重比你年轻的人，你可能会做得很好。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: I think we're moving into, there's a book that David Epstein wrote called Range, and the whole premise of range is that we are moving out of the era of the specialists and into the era of the generalists. I think AI is just accelerating this. As we are more reliant upon AI, and AI can be exceptional at technical skills and solutions really expeditiously, I think generalists, people who can think broadly, become all the more important. I think that what I would say to someone in HR or recruiting is beyond what I already said before, is the person passionate? (00:36:23): Are they curious? Are they a learner? Do they have good energy? I would also say, are they a generalist when they're a problem solver? I actually think that's going to be an increasingly important part of how effective companies think broadly. I think that's a key one. I think also, this idea of how do you create intergenerational collaboration in the form of mutual mentorships? One of the things I loved at Airbnb, there were a few people I did this with, where I had something to teach them and they had something to teach me. (00:37:02): A good example, my iPhone, so there's 97% of the utility of my iPhone that I probably don't use and don't know how to use. This was back in, let's say, 2013, 2014. There were people who knew iPhone or Google Suites back then. I'd never used a Google Doc back then when I joined Airbnb. There were people who could teach me something technical, and then they wanted to learn something from me, which would be like, "How do you want a great meeting," or, "How do you give a great employee review?" There are a lot of managers who've never been a manager before. (00:37:45): How do you disperse people like me in the organization so that there's usually not enough time for these young managers to come to some training session on how to do a good employee review. You sort of have to do it out there in the field. It's like apprenticeship back in the trades. You're an electrician apprentice, not because you're watching some video on it, you're out there in the field, doing it. That's a huge value in a younger company when you have some older people who have not been vested with the responsibility of managing those younger people. (00:38:23): They may actually be reporting to someone younger than them, but they're there to actually be support. In some ways, I think that was part of the unexpected value that I was able to offer to Airbnb and to Brian specifically, because there are a ton of people in Airbnb who were not even in my departments who would come to me and say, "I'm having a problem. How do I solve this? Can we spend lunch together?" I almost always said yes.
turns.zh: 我认为我们正在进入大卫·爱泼斯坦写的一本名为《范围》的书，《范围》的整个前提是我们正在走出专家时代，进入通才时代。我认为人工智能只是加速了这一过程。由于我们更加依赖人工智能，并且人工智能可以非常迅速地在技术技能和解决方案方面表现出色，我认为通才、能够广泛思考的人变得更加重要。我认为我要对人力资源或招聘人员说的话超出了我之前所说的范围，这个人是否充满激情？ (00:36:23)：他们好奇吗？他们是学习者吗？他们有良好的能量吗？我还想说，当他们是问题解决者时，他们是多面手吗？事实上，我认为这将成为高效公司广泛思考的一个越来越重要的部分。我认为这是关键之一。我还认为，如何以相互指导的形式建立代际合作？我在 Airbnb 喜欢的一件事是，我和一些人一起做这件事，我可以教他们一些东西，他们也可以教我一些东西。 (00:37:02)：一个很好的例子，我的 iPhone，所以我的 iPhone 97% 的实用功能我可能不会使用，也不知道如何使用。那是在 2013 年、2014 年。当时有人知道 iPhone 或 Google Suites。当我加入 Airbnb 时，我从未使用过 Google Doc。有些人可以教我一些技术知识，然后他们想向我学习一些东西，比如“你想要一次精彩的会议”，或者“你如何给员工一个精彩的评价？”有很多经理以前从未当过经理。 (00:37:45)：如何将像我这样的人分散在组织中，以便这些年轻的经理通常没有足够的时间来参加一些关于如何进行良好的员工审查的培训课程。你必须在现场做这件事。这就像回到行业中的学徒期。你是一名电工学徒，不是因为你在看一些视频，而是因为你在现场，正在做这件事。这对于年轻的公司来说是一个巨大的价值，因为你有一些年长的人，而他们没有被赋予管理这些年轻人的责任。 (00:38:23)：他们实际上可能是在向比自己年轻的人汇报，但他们实际上是在提供支持。在某些方面，我认为这是我能够为 Airbnb 和 Brian 提供的意外价值的一部分，因为 Airbnb 中有很多人甚至不属于我的部门，他们会来找我说：“我遇到了问题。我该如何解决这个问题？我们可以一起吃午餐吗？”我几乎总是说是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think the reason people did that in many ways is you just have a very unique aura of wisdom, and it's hard to replicate that, Chip.
turns.zh: 我认为人们在很多方面这样做的原因是你有一种非常独特的智慧光环，这是很难复制的，奇普。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yes, and it all comes back to the curiosity. If I was just the older elder, dispensing wisdom, people would've gotten bored very quickly. I think the fact, yeah, I was on the board of Burning Man, that's cool. I show up as someone who feels younger than I am. I'm turning 65 this year. The bottom line is I think people lost track of my age, partly because I lost track of my age.
turns.zh: 是的，这一切都回到了好奇心。如果我只是年长的长辈，传播智慧，人们很快就会感到无聊。我认为事实上，是的，我是火人节的董事会成员，这很酷。我表现得比我年轻。我今年就 65 岁了。最重要的是，我认为人们忘记了我的年龄，部分原因是我忘记了自己的年龄。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such good advice on the front end to be successful as a person kind of getting older in tech is curiosity, positive energy, the way you talked about it, passionate, engagement, is that the term?
turns.zh: 对于前端来说，这是一个很好的建议，作为一个在科技领域长大的人，要想取得成功，就需要好奇心、正能量，就像你所说的那样，热情、参与，是这个词吗？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then on the other side is hire generalists. This actually comes up a lot in the AI conversations, just exactly as you said, the power of generalists reminds me, I'm going to this gym now, and the lady there is just like, "I love AI so much, because I'm just such a big picture person, and I am so bad at just getting, thinking about the details, and AI solves all that for me." It's like, "Here, here's what I want to do. I'll do this, move my house to here, here." It's like, "Here's what you need to do, step one, two, three, four, five."
turns.zh: 另一方面是聘请多面手。这实际上在人工智能对话中经常出现，正如你所说，通才的力量提醒我，我现在要去这个健身房，那里的女士就像是，“我非常喜欢人工智能，因为我只是一个大局观的人，而且我很不擅长获取、思考细节，而人工智能为我解决了所有这些问题。”就像，“这里，这就是我想做的事。我会这样做，把我的房子搬到这里，这里。”就像，“这就是你需要做的，第一步、第二步、第三步、第四步、第五步。”

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: It is remarkable. Since the time I've known you, how fast it has become dominant in our lives. Yeah, I think one of the last thing I'd say is, look, I'm privileged. For those of you who are listening or watching this and you're saying, "Well, Chip, you were 52 years old and they came to you. That doesn't happen to me. I'm not in that position." The thing I would say is, you're right, but I could have been plucked and brought in and partly as Brian's boy, people would've rejected me, because if I didn't show up the right way, it wouldn't have worked well. (00:41:00): There are lots of people who Brian brought into the company who didn't work well. I think the key is how do you get the foot in the door? At the end of the day, those second and third order of degrees of separation in terms of networking are still essential. The most important thing is to be able to articulate what you have accomplished in a new way that a recruiter says, "Wow." I really tell people I would love to see a resume. (00:41:41): First of all, the question that I think it was, who was it? Someone asked it, I don't remember if it was Cheryl Stamberg or someone else asked her, who said, "What's the biggest problem you're dealing with here, and how can I help you?" That's a great line. Number two is what I love to see is not so much what roles you've had, what bullet points do you have of your things you've learned? Give me, in a paragraph, a thorny problem you faced. What was the problem, and what skills you used to actually accomplish it, and what was the result of that? (00:42:22): I would love to see a resume like that. The older you are, the more you can actually have a resume like that. Then you can use that as the conversation piece when you're doing interviews.
turns.zh: 这是非常了不起的。自从我认识你以来，它很快就在我们的生活中占据了主导地位。是的，我想我要说的最后一件事是，看，我很荣幸。对于那些正在听或正在观看此节目的人来说，您会说：“好吧，奇普，您已经 52 岁了，他们来找您。这不会发生在我身上。我不处于那个位置。”我想说的是，你是对的，但我可能会被选拔并带进来，部分作为布莱恩的儿子，人们会拒绝我，因为如果我没有以正确的方式出现，那就不会有很好的效果。 (00:41:00)：布莱恩带进公司的很多人都表现不佳。我认为关键是如何迈入这扇门？归根结底，网络方面的第二和第三级分离度仍然至关重要。最重要的是能够以招聘人员说“哇”的新方式阐明你所取得的成就。我真的告诉​​人们我很想看到简历。 (00:41:41)：首先，我认为的问题是谁？有人问过，我不记得是谢丽尔·斯坦伯格还是其他人问过她，她说：“你在这里面临的最大问题是什么，我能帮你什么？”这是一条很棒的线。第二，我喜欢看到的并不是你所扮演的角色，而是你对所学到的东西有哪些要点？用一段话告诉我你遇到的一个棘手问题。问题是什么，你用什么技能来实际完成它，结果是什么？ (00:42:22)：我很想看到这样的简历。你年纪越大，你就越能拥有这样的简历。然后你可以在面试时将其用作对话片段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I love that we're getting into interview advice and resume advice.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。我喜欢我们提供面试建议和简历建议。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of thorny problems, and also why Brian decided to reach out to you, I want to go back to the beginning of your career.
turns.zh: 说到棘手的问题，以及布莱恩为什么决定联系你，我想回到你职业生涯的开始。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right out of business-
turns.zh: 刚下业-

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: You're good at this, by the way. You're good at this.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，你很擅长这个。你很擅长这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was thinking ahead. Okay, so you're in business school, you left business school, you're like, "Maybe I should start a hotel." Something that rarely works out usually probably leads to a lot of money lost and a lot of frustration and just like, "Okay, what have I done with my life?" Worked out for you. (00:43:07): Ended up building the second largest boutique hotel chain in the world, Joie de Vivre, beloved. I loved every single experience I've had as Joie de Vivre. When you sold it, I was like, "That is so sad." Talk about just that story. I know this could go on for hours, but what's the-
turns.zh: 我正在提前思考。好吧，所以你在商学院，你离开商学院，你会想，“也许我应该开一家酒店。”一些很少成功的事情通常可能会导致大量金钱损失和很多挫败感，就像“好吧，我这辈子做了什么？”为你锻炼了。 (00:43:07)：最终建成了世界第二大精品连锁酒店 Joie de Vivre，深受喜爱。我喜欢作为 Joie de Vivre 的每一次经历。当你卖掉它时，我想，“这太悲伤了。”只谈那个故事。我知道这可能会持续几个小时，但那是-

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah, I'll be brief.
turns.zh: 是的，我会简短地说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: 26 years old, couple of years out of Stanford Business School, working for a commercial real estate developer. I was bored silly. I wanted to do something more creative. Bill Graham, famous concert promoter, said to me, because I had gotten to know him, "What San Francisco really needs is a rock and roll hotel." I decided to start looking to find a broken down motel hotel that I could turn into a rock and roll hotel. (00:43:46): I found something in the Tenderloin, and turned it into the Phoenix, which became a famous rock and roll hotel that I have owned for 39 years now. Long story short is that was how I started Joie de Vivre, the company. We grew to 52 hotels around California, became the second largest, as you said, in the world in terms of the number of hotels, boutique hotels that we operated. I loved it till I hated it. In my late forties, I hated it, didn't want to do it anymore. The great recession came along and it was just kicking my ass. (00:44:23): I really went through a bit of what I now call a midlife chrysalis, but a midlife crisis, where I just wanted to change everything. I got through it. I had an NDE, I had a near-death experience where I had an allergic reaction to an antibiotic and I died. From that point forward, I realized every day is a gift and a bonus, and I decided to sell my company at the bottom of the great recession. That's really how I created this space in my life to be able to join Airbnb.
turns.zh: 26 岁，从斯坦福商学院毕业几年，在一家商业房地产开发商工作。我无聊傻了。我想做一些更有创意的事情。著名音乐会发起人比尔·格雷厄姆（Bill Graham）在我认识他后对我说：“旧金山真正需要的是一家摇滚酒店。”我决定开始寻找一家破旧的汽车旅馆酒店，我可以将其改造成一家摇滚酒店。 (00:43:46)：我在 Tenderloin 找到了一些东西，然后把它变成了 Phoenix，它成为了一家著名的摇滚酒店，我已经拥有了 39 年了。长话短说，我就是这样创办了 Joie de Vivre 公司的。我们在加州各地的酒店数量增加到了 52 家，正如您所说，就我们经营的酒店、精品酒店的数量而言，我们成为世界第二大酒店。我喜欢它直到我讨厌它。在我四十多岁的时候，我讨厌它，不想再这样做了。大衰退来了，这让我很受打击。 (00:44:23)：我确实经历了一些我现在所说的中年蛹，而是一场中年危机，我只想改变一切。我熬过来了。我有过一次濒死体验，有过一次濒死体验，我对抗生素产生了过敏反应，然后就死了。从那时起，我意识到每一天都是一份礼物和奖金，我决定在经济大衰退的底部卖掉我的公司。这就是我在生活中创造这个空间以便能够加入 Airbnb 的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let's back up a little bit. This near-death experience, share more there. What happened there?
turns.zh: 好吧，让我们稍微备份一下。这种濒临死亡的经历，还有更多分享。那里发生了什么？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah, so I write books. I've written seven or eight books, and I had written a book called Peak: How Great Companies Get Their Mojo from Maslow. It was a book that Brian really liked, and part of the reason he wanted to reach out to me. I was on a book tour, I had a broken ankle. I broke my ankle at a bachelor party playing baseball. I ended up with a cut on my leg and the cut on my leg had fertilizer in it and went septic. I was on a very strong antibiotic and I died. (00:45:39): I went flatlined from the allergic reaction to the antibiotic. I saw, it happened nine times over 90 minutes, I kept dying, kept flatlining, yeah. Ended up in the hospital for three days. They finally said, "Listen, it's an allergic reaction, we believe." They thought it was a heart attack, a bunch of stuff, stroke, et cetera. No, it was the allergic reaction. I saw birds. I saw all this beautiful stuff. We don't have time to go into it.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我写书。我已经写了七八本书，其中有一本书叫《巅峰：伟大的公司如何从马斯洛那里获得魔力》。布莱恩非常喜欢这本书，这也是他想联系我的部分原因。我当时正在巡回售书，脚踝骨折了。我在单身派对上打棒球时扭伤了脚踝。最后我的腿上被割伤了，腿上的伤口里有化肥，然后化脓了。我服用了很强的抗生素，结果我死了。 (00:45:39)：我因对抗生素的过敏反应而变得平淡。我看到，这种情况在 90 分钟内发生了九次，我一直在死，一直在平淡，是的。结果在医院住了三天。他们最后说：“听着，我们相信这是过敏反应。”他们认为这是心脏病发作、一堆东西、中风等等。不，这是过敏反应。我看到了鸟。我看到了所有这些美丽的东西。我们没有时间去深究。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You did? What?
turns.zh: 你做到了吗？什么？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: I did. You want to hear this? Yeah, I saw this beautiful stuff.
turns.zh: 我做到了。你想听这个吗？是的，我看到了这么漂亮的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 我们开始做吧。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: I think there's a hotel in San Francisco called the Vitale that I built across the street from the ferry building, and it's still there, but it's no longer called the Vitale. In that hotel, there were these slippers in every guest room. One slipper said slow, the other slipper said down. I was wearing these slippers in my flatline thing, flying in the air in a 40-foot tall living room in the Alps, surrounded by birds that were tweeting and chirping at me. (00:46:50): I understood bird talk. I understand exactly what they were saying. They kept telling me, "If you slow down, you will see beauty and you will see awe." There was a bunch of other things, but let me just limit it to that and just say, and then the birds would say, "It's time to go." The birds would go out the big window into the mountains, and I would try to follow them. Right as I would get to the window, all of a sudden, I'd come back to life.
turns.zh: 我想在旧金山有一家名为 Vitale 的酒店，是我在渡轮大楼对面建造的，它仍然在那里，但不再叫 Vitale。在那家酒店里，每间客房都有这样的拖鞋。一只拖鞋表示慢，另一只拖鞋表示向下。我穿着这双拖鞋，在阿尔卑斯山一间 40 英尺高的客厅里飞翔，周围都是对我鸣叫的鸟儿。 (00:46:50)：我听懂了鸟语。我完全明白他们在说什么。他们一直告诉我，“如果你放慢脚步，你会看到美丽，你会看到敬畏。”还有很多其他的事情，但让我仅限于此，然后说，然后鸟儿会说：“是时候离开了。”鸟儿会从大窗户飞到山里，我会试着跟着它们。就在我走到窗边时，突然间，我又活过来了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Holy shit. I love that there was a message inside of this experience. I don't know how many people experienced that. Clearly, this led to a big life change. It's interesting that a lot of times, you need something like that. You've been doing this for how many years at that point? Running Joie de Vivre?
turns.zh: 天哪。我喜欢这次经历中传达的信息。我不知道有多少人经历过这样的事情。显然，这导致了生活的巨大改变。有趣的是，很多时候，你需要这样的东西。那时你已经这样做了多少年了？运行Joie de Vivre？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: At that point, I'd been running Joie de Vivre for 22 years.
turns.zh: 那时，我已经经营 Joie de Vivre 22 年了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 22 years. It's interesting that you need something like that a lot of times. Otherwise, it just momentum just keeps carrying you forward.
turns.zh: 22年。有趣的是，你很多时候都需要类似的东西。否则，它只是推动你前进的动力。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Within two years, I'd sold it, and I had the chance to move on.
turns.zh: 两年之内，我卖掉了它，我有机会继续前进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With building Joie de Vivre, something you've written about a number of times is just the way you built it is a really unique approach to building a business. Specifically, there's a huge focus on culture, which also came out at Airbnb. Talk about just why you see culture as such an important part of how you build a business like tangibly. A lot of people talk about culture, warm, fuzzy stuff, but you think about it very tangibly.
turns.zh: 通过构建 Joie de Vivre，您已经多次写过的内容就是您构建它的方式，这是一种非常独特的业务创建方法。具体来说，Airbnb 也非常注重文化。谈谈为什么你认为文化是你如何建立有形企业的重要组成部分。很多人谈论文化、温暖、模糊的东西，但你思考得非常具体。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Culture is what happens around here when the boss is not around. The more distributed a company, the more culture is important. The boss is around in a traditional bricks and mortar workplace where everybody shows up at eight and leaves at six, and we all see each other. In my company, in Joie de Vivre, we had 52 hotels, and 25 restaurants, and four spas, and it was distributed. I couldn't be in all those places all the time. (00:48:52): Similarly, with Airbnb, Airbnb had offices around the world and it was a global company. The more distributed you are, of course, in the remote work world we live in, the more culture is important, and more difficult. When you're remote, there's these few cues you have about how we do things around here. They're usually in a digital, virtual format, which is why it's all the more important for you to have in-person gatherings of a team more often if you are virtual. (00:49:27): At the end of the day, the reason the culture is important is because it actually helps, it helps guide people in terms of making decisions, but it's also a magnet for the right kind of people. Oracle has a different culture than Apple, which has a different culture than Facebook. You can choose the place you're going to work based upon the culture. There are people who can be very good at what they do, but if they're in the wrong culture, they're in the wrong kind of environment, and they're not willing to shift to fit that culture. (00:50:01): We saw it at Airbnb all over and over again. In fact, Airbnb saw it, I think when with Amazon people. Apple people have resonated pretty well at Airbnb, Amazon people, less so. Those are two different cultures, Amazon and Apple. Therefore, understanding a culture before you even actually take the job is one of the more important decisions you need to make is like, "Is this culture a culture that I can live with and maybe influence?" There's language about culture fit. (00:50:37): I like to say culture add, because culture fit to me can actually be quite negative toward somebody who is the aberration. You have to fit in. Especially if this is a demographic thing, a person of color, a gay person, a person in a wheelchair, so you have to fit in. A culture add suggests that actually having some diversity on the team is helpful, because it actually adds to the culture. You still have to be able to get along in that culture. Culture is an intangible. That's the problem with it is it's hard to measure, but you see its value and you understand whether it's working based upon employee pulse reports and things like that.
turns.zh: 文化是老板不在的时候发生的事情。公司分布越广，文化就越重要。老板在传统的实体工作场所，每个人八点上班，六点下班，我们都会见面。在我的公司 Joie de Vivre，我们拥有 52 家酒店、25 家餐厅和 4 个水疗中心，并且是分布式的。我不可能一直呆在那些地方。 (00:48:52)：与 Airbnb 类似，Airbnb 在世界各地设有办事处，是一家全球性公司。当然，在我们生活的远程工作世界中，你的分布越分散，文化就越重要，也就越困难。当您身处偏远地区时，您可以通过以下一些线索了解我们如何在这里做事。它们通常采用数字虚拟形式，这就是为什么如果您是虚拟的，那么更频繁地进行团队面对面聚会就显得尤为重要。 (00:49:27)：归根结底，文化之所以重要，是因为它确实有帮助，它有助于指导人们做出决策，而且它也能吸引合适的人。甲骨文与苹果有着不同的文化，而苹果也与 Facebook 有着不同的文化。您可以根据文化选择要工作的地方。有些人可以非常擅长自己所做的事情，但如果他们处于错误的文化中，他们就处于错误的环境中，并且他们不愿意转变以适应这种文化。 (00:50:01)：我们在 Airbnb 上一遍又一遍地看到它。事实上，我想 Airbnb 在与亚马逊员工合作时就看到了这一点。苹果员工在 Airbnb 上的反响很好，而亚马逊员工的反响则较差。这是两种不同的文化，亚马逊和苹果。因此，在你真正接受工作之前了解一种文化是你需要做出的更重要的决定之一，比如“这种文化是我可以忍受并可能影响的文化吗？”有关于文化契合度的语言。 (00:50:37)：我喜欢说文化补充，因为适合我的文化实际上对那些异常的人来说可能是相当负面的。你必须融入。特别是如果这是一个人口统计问题，有色人种、同性恋者、坐轮椅的人，所以你必须融入。文化补充表明，团队中实际上具有一定的多样性是有帮助的，因为它实际上增加了文化。你仍然必须能够在那种文化中相处。文化是一种无形的东西。这就是它的问题在于它很难衡量，但你可以看到它的价值，并且你可以根据员工脉搏报告等了解它是否有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talk about having to understand the culture is such a key part of having success at a company. Do you have any advice for just how to understand the culture for someone interviewing? I don't know. You came in, you work part-time, it's easier to experience it all. Any tips there for, "Okay, this is for me, it's not for me?"
turns.zh: 您谈到必须了解文化是公司取得成功的关键部分。对于如何理解面试者的文化，您有什么建议吗？我不知道。你进来了，你兼职工作，更容易体验这一切。对于“好吧，这是给我的，这不是给我的？”有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: When you're interviewing, you're also interviewing them. When you're interviewing, it's not about you having to prove yourself. It's also for them to actually prove themselves as a company, and also try to understand if there is some alignment in the company. The kind of questions I would ask as someone who's being interviewed would be, what are three to five adjectives that define this culture? What's the biggest problem in this culture, in terms of something that's just endemic or baked in across the organization? (00:52:14): Is it ever going to get fixed? How could I come in and maybe help that? Which frankly, at a very junior level, you're not going to be able to help it except for in very minor ways. If you're a senior person, you might be able to help it. Those are the kind of questions I'd want to know. Frankly, if I'm asking that same question about what are the adjectives to multiple people, am I hearing the same thing over and over again? If I'm not, is that because there's not alignment? Is that because different departments have different flavors? (00:52:48): You could have a culture within a department that's very different than the overall corporate culture. The corporate culture certainly has an enormous oppressive influence, but you can be in a culture, a really great culture of a team or a department, in an overall company culture that's not good. In the long run, that oppressive company culture is either going to have to evolv,e or your department, you may lose people.
turns.zh: 当你面试时，你也在面试他们。当你面试时，并不是要证明自己。他们还可以真正证明自己是一家公司，并尝试了解公司是否存在某种一致性。作为接受采访的人，我会问的问题是，定义这种文化的三到五个形容词是什么？就整个组织中流行或根深蒂固的问题而言，这种文化中最大的问题是什么？ (00:52:14)：它会得到修复吗？我怎么能进来帮忙呢？坦率地说，在非常初级的水平上，除了非常小的方面之外，你将无法帮助它。如果你是一位资深人士，也许可以提供帮助。这些都是我想知道的问题。坦率地说，如果我问同样的问题，关于多个人的形容词是什么，我是否会一遍又一遍地听到同样的事情？如果不是，是不是因为没有对齐？是因为不同的部门有不同的口味吗？ (00:52:48)：部门内的文化可能与整体企业文化截然不同。企业文化当然具有巨大的压迫性影响，但你可能处于一种文化中，一个团队或一个部门的真正伟大的文化中，但整体的公司文化并不好。从长远来看，这种压迫性的公司文化要么必须发展，要么你的部门可能会失去人员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I reflect back on the impact you had at Airbnb, one of the funny things I think about is triangles showing up a lot on decks, and specifically rooted in Maslow's hierarchy, just like everything's this Maslow hierarchy metaphor.
turns.zh: 当我回顾你们对 Airbnb 的影响时，我想到的一件有趣的事情是三角形在甲板上大量出现，并且特别植根于马斯洛层次结构，就像一切都是马斯洛层次结构隐喻一样。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: True.
turns.zh: 真的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This one, I don't know, specific piece of this is you have this kind of model you think about for how to help employees be successful at a company. It's kind of rooted in your Peak book philosophy. Maybe just talk about that, and then if there's anything else you want to expand on with this power of thinking through the Maslow hierarchy.
turns.zh: 我不知道，具体的一点是你有这样一种模型，你正在考虑如何帮助员工在公司取得成功。它有点植根于你的 Peak 书籍哲学。也许只是谈论这一点，然后如果您还想通过马斯洛层次思维的力量来扩展其他任何内容。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Maslow's hierarchy, basically five levels. Later in life, he had a seven and an eight level model, but at the base is the kind of physical, water, food, air, and you move up to self-actualization at the top. To use this model as a hierarchy of needs for employees, customers, and investors is what the Peak model is about. The Peak, my book. The employee model is really simple. It's money or compensation at the base, recognition in the middle, and meaning at the top. (00:54:39): Now, there are some industries and some kinds of jobs in which money is 90% of the pyramid. Just because of the base doesn't mean it's not the dominant part of the pyramid, but the differentiation often is in recognition and meaning. In nonprofits, usually the money piece of it's rather thin. The recognition's this, and meaning's huge. Understanding how do you create an organization, and I gave a TED Talk in 2010 about this topic as well, how do you measure the intangibles of meaning and how do you create an environment where people feel a sense of meaning? (00:55:18): The customer pyramid, briefly, I'll just say that one, is meeting expectations is the base, meeting desires is in the middle, and then meeting unrecognized needs. I think one of the things that we did at Airbnb about a year after I joined, and when Jonathan Goldenhall was joining, is we really tried to ask ourselves, "Are we in the home sharing business, or are we in some kind of business that is even bigger and broader than that?" Ultimately, we came up with the idea that we were in the belong anywhere business. (00:55:49): Airbnb was not in home sharing, we were in belonging anywhere. Once you have that down, that was sort of the unrecognized need at the top of the pyramid. Then that becomes an organizing principle for how do you teach your hosts to create a sense of belonging? How does our marketing and advertising play up the belonging piece, especially and the everywhere piece, because hotels are not everywhere, but homes are? I would just say that this model, the idea of hierarchies is, I think, very helpful. Yeah, my book Peak has been around for 18 years, but I still am asked to give 20 or 30 speeches a year on it.
turns.zh: 马斯洛的层次结构，基本上有五个层次。在后来的生活中，他有一个七级和八级模型，但底层是身体、水、食物、空气，然后你会上升到顶层的自我实现。使用这个模型作为员工、客户和投资者的需求层次结构就是峰值模型的目的。 《山顶》，我的书。员工模型非常简单。底层是金钱或补偿，中间是认可，顶层是意义。 (00:54:39)：现在，在某些行业和某些工作中，金钱占据了金字塔的 90%。仅仅因为基础并不意味着它不是金字塔的主导部分，但差异通常在于认知和意义。在非营利组织中，通常所获得的资金相当薄弱。认可就是这样，意义重大。了解如何创建一个组织，我在 2010 年的 TED 演讲中也谈到了这个主题，如何衡量无形的意义以及如何创建一个让人们感受到意义的环境？ (00:55:18)：客户金字塔，简单来说，我只想说一，满足期望是基础，满足欲望是中间，然后是满足未识别的需求。我认为，在我加入 Airbnb 大约一年后，当乔纳森·戈登霍尔 (Jonathan Goldenhall) 加入时，我们所做的一件事是，我们真的试着问自己：“我们是在从事房屋共享业务，还是在从事某种比这更大、更广泛的业务？”最终，我们想到了我们从事“归属于任何地方”的业务。 (00:55:49)：Airbnb 并不属于家庭共享，我们在任何地方都有归属感。一旦你明白了这一点，这就是金字塔顶端未被认识到的需求。那么这就成为你如何教导主人创造归属感的组织原则？我们的营销和广告如何突出归属感，尤其是无处不在的部分，因为酒店不是无处不在，但家却无处不在？我只想说，我认为这种模型、层次结构的想法非常有帮助。是的，我的书《巅峰》已经问世 18 年了，但我仍然被要求每年就这本书发表 20 到 30 场演讲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. This pyramid of comp, recognition, meaning is really interesting, especially these days, because with all this AI researcher poaching, there's all this talk of just like, "Will people just go work wherever they get the most money, or is there a mission and meaning to the work they're doing that will keep them not taking a hundred million dollars offer?" Seems to be happening in a lot of cases, which shows you the power of meaning.
turns.zh: 哦，伙计。这个由报酬、认可、意义组成的金字塔真的很有趣，尤其是在现在，因为随着人工智能研究人员的挖角，人们都在谈论“人们会去能赚最多钱的地方工作，还是他们正在做的工作有一个使命和意义，让他们不会接受一亿美元的工作？”似乎在很多情况下都在发生，这让你看到了意义的力量。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah. If you know you're working for a toxic company, at some point, your conscience kicks in. Whether it's toxic in terms of the purpose of the company, toxic in terms of the leadership or the culture, life is too short.
turns.zh: 是的。如果你知道自己在一家有毒的公司工作，那么在某些时候，你的良心就会开始起作用。无论是从公司的宗旨来看，还是从领导层或文化方面来说，这都是有毒的，生命太短暂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. You've had two major shifts in your career. You started the hotel chain, then you went to Airbnb. Most recently, the Airbnb experience, I imagine, led you to starting something called the Modern Elder Academy. Talk about what is the Modern Elder Academy?
turns.zh: 好的。您的职业生涯经历了两次重大转变。你创办了连锁酒店，然后又去了 Airbnb。最近，我想，Airbnb 的经历让您创办了一个名为“现代老年学院”的机构。谈谈什么是现代老年学院？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah, what is going on with that Modern Elder Academy? The Modern Elder Academy. There was a couple times where I was called the Modern Elder at Airbnb, and then I was told that a Modern Elder is someone who's as curious as they are wise. Jonathan Mildenhall, who is the chief marketing officer at Airbnb, used to call me the Modern Elder as well, and he said, "If you ever create a school, Modern Elder would be a good name." (00:57:56): We talked about it, and next thing I knew, I was saying, "Okay, this is called the Modern Elder Academy." We now call it MEA because elder is a fraught word on some level, it makes you sound elderly. What I really wanted to create was a place where people could come and do a workshop, they're five day workshops in Baja on the beach, or in Santa Fe on a big four square mile horse ranch, and reimagine and repurpose yourself, and navigate transitions. (00:58:27): We go through so many transitions in the middle of our life, let's say between, I define midlife as 35 to 75, guys. It's a very long life stage. We go through a lot of transitions. We are constantly evolving our purpose. We're building our wisdom. We have knowledge management tools out there, but we're the wisdom management tools. We're the tools that help us to get wiser over time, and then we need to reframe our relationship with getting older. Becca Levy has shown at Yale that when you shift your mindset on aging from a negative to a positive, you get seven and a half years of additional life, which is more life than any other biohack that's being done right now. (00:59:08): That's what we do, and we have 7,000 grads from 60 countries, and 56 regional chapters around the world. It's a bit of a movement, and I teach. I teach some of the workshops, and we have all kinds of famous people who come and teach. For me, creating the world's first midlife wisdom school just feels like the natural next thing for me to do. I love hospitality, so it's a very upscale kind of experience, but we have scholarships. I love retreat centers. I was on the board of the Esalen Institute in Big Sur for 10 years. I love wellness. (00:59:45): I've owned the Kabuki Springs and Spa for 28 years, which is the largest spa in San Francisco, and I love education. My book, Wisdom at Work: The Making of a Modern Elder, gave me a curriculum in which we've expanded quite a bit with Harvard, Yale, Stanford, and UC, Berkeley professors helping us create a curriculum around midlife. That's how MEA came about.
turns.zh: 是啊，那个现代长老学院到底是怎么回事？现代老年学院。有几次，我在 Airbnb 被称为“现代长者”，然后我被告知，“现代长者”是一个既好奇又聪明的人。 Airbnb 的首席营销官乔纳森·米尔登霍尔 (Jonathan Mildenhall) 也曾叫我“现代长者”，他说：“如果你要创建一所学校，“现代长者”将是一个好名字。” (00:57:56)：我们讨论过，接下来我就说，“好吧，这就是现代长者学院。”我们现在称之为“MEA”，因为“长辈”在某种程度上是一个令人担忧的词，它让你听起来很老。我真正想创造的是一个人们可以来参加研讨会的地方，他们在巴哈的海滩上或在圣达菲的一个四平方英里的大马场上举办为期五天的研讨会，重新想象和重新定位自己，并导航过渡。 (00:58:27)：我们在中年经历了很多转变，比如说，我将中年定义为 35 岁到 75 岁，伙计们。这是一个非常漫长的人生阶段。我们经历了很多转变。我们不断发展我们的目标。我们正在培养我们的智慧。我们有知识管理工具，但我们是智慧管理工具。我们是帮助我们随着时间的推移变得更加明智的工具，然后我们需要重新构建我们与变老的关系。贝卡·利维（Becca Levy）在耶鲁大学的研究表明，当你将自己对衰老的看法从消极转向积极时，你就会多活七年半，这比目前正在进行的任何其他生物黑客技术都长。 (00:59:08)：这就是我们所做的，我们拥有来自 60 个国家/地区的 7,000 名毕业生，在全球设有 56 个地区分会。这是一个小小的运动，我教。我在一些研讨会上授课，我们有各种各样的名人来授课。对我来说，创建世界上第一所中年智慧学校感觉就像是我接下来要做的自然而然的事情。我喜欢热情好客，所以这是一种非常高档的体验，但我们有奖学金。我喜欢静修中心。我在大苏尔伊莎兰研究所 (Esalen Institute) 的董事会任职了 10 年。我热爱健康。 (00:59:45)：我拥有 Kabuki Springs and Spa 已有 28 年了，这是旧金山最大的水疗中心，我热爱教育。我的书《工作中的智慧：现代老年人的塑造》为我提供了一个课程，我们在哈佛大学、耶鲁大学、斯坦福大学、加州大学伯克利分校的教授帮助我们创建围绕中年的课程的基础上进行了相当多的扩展。 MEA 就是这样诞生的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To your point, I forget who said, I think you said Jonathan has said this was a natural next step for you, I completely agree. It's like, looking back, this is the obvious thing you should be doing right now.
turns.zh: 对于你的观点，我忘记是谁说的，我想你说乔纳森已经说过这对你来说是自然的下一步，我完全同意。回想起来，这显然是你现在应该做的事情。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, I'm learning more things about you. I didn't know you were involved with the Kabuki Spa. I think Esalen and I knew, you just keep getting more interested.
turns.zh: 另外，我对你的了解也越来越多。我不知道你参与了歌舞伎水疗中心。我想伊莎伦和我都知道，你只是越来越感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple threads here I want to actually follow. This point you made about shifting your mindset to aging as a positive thing helps you live longer. That's such a powerful point. Can you just speak more to that, just what does that look like?
turns.zh: 这里有几个我想真正关注的主题。您提出的这一点是关于将您的心态转变为衰老，因为积极的事情可以帮助您活得更久。这是一个非常有力的观点。你能多说一点吗，那是什么样子的？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Yeah, there's lots of data points. I'll talk about two. One is this Becca Levy study, which has been going on for 15 to 20 years. If you sort of buy into the ageism of American society or Hallmark cards, when you get a card at age 40, 50, or beyond, there's a belief that life gets worse as you get older. If you can survive your midlife crisis, all you have to look forward to is disease, decrepitude, and death. The bottom line is there's a lot of things that get better with age. I wrote a book called Learning to Love Midlife. (01:01:20): The subtitle says it all: 12 Reasons Why Life Gets Better with Age. What I really wanted to do with that book, which is really, it summarizes the MEA curriculum, I wanted to write a book that sort of helped people to see the upside of aging, the unexpected pleasures of aging. They had a pro-aging, not just an anti-aging point of view. When you actually have a pro-aging point of view and you see the upside of aging, you take better care of yourself, both your mind and your body. You actually are willing to learn and try new things. (01:01:51): One of my favorite MEA questions is, 10 years from now, what will you regret if you don't learn it or do it now? It's a powerful question, really important question as we get older. When you're young, you've got all of your life left ahead of you. When I moved to Baja part-time in Mexico at age 56, I had a mindset which was, "I'm too old to learn Spanish. I'm too old to learn to surf," but when I said, "10 years from now, what will I regret if I don't learn it or it now?" I said, "Well, 10 years from now, I might still be living in Baja. I should learn Spanish, I should learn how to surf because we're right next to a surf break." (01:02:29): I did. What I believe is that anticipated regret is a form of wisdom, and it's a catalyst for taking action. That's one data point. The other data point is something called the U-curve of happiness, and it's been around for 20 years, and it shows the following. It has changed in the last couple of years because young adults are unhappy like never before. A 20 or a 22-year-old, really unhappy, 24-year-old, really unhappy. (01:02:58): Historically, the way it was is you were happy from 18 to 23 or 24, and then around 23 or 24, you start to see a long, slow decline in life satisfaction that actually bottoms out between 45 and 50. I'm sorry to tell you that, Lenny, since you're 44, but your mileage may vary.
turns.zh: 是的，有很多数据点。我就讲两个吧。其中一项是 Becca Levy 的研究，该研究已经持续了 15 到 20 年。如果你接受了美国社会或 Hallmark 卡的年龄歧视，那么当你在 40 岁、50 岁或更老的时候拿到一张卡时，你就会相信，随着年龄的增长，生活会变得更糟。如果你能度过中年危机，你所期待的就是疾病、衰老和死亡。最重要的是，随着年龄的增长，很多事情都会变得更好。我写了一本书，叫《学会爱中年》。 (01:01:20)：副标题说明了一切：随着年龄的增长，生活变得更好的 12 个原因。我真正想用那本书做什么，它总结了 MEA 课程，我想写一本帮助人们看到衰老的好处，看到衰老带来的意想不到的乐趣。他们有促进衰老的观点，而不仅仅是抗衰老的观点。当你真正持有支持衰老的观点并且看到衰老的好处时，你就会更好地照顾自己，包括你的思想和身体。你实际上愿意学习和尝试新事物。 (01:01:51)：我最喜欢的 MEA 问题之一是，10 年后，如果你现在不学习或不做，你会后悔什么？这是一个有力的问题，随着我们年龄的增长，这个问题非常重要。当你还年轻的时候，你的一生都还剩下。当我 56 岁时兼职搬到墨西哥巴哈时，我的心态是，“我太老了，学不了西班牙语。我太老了，学不了冲浪。”但是当我说，“10 年后，如果我不学或者现在不学，我会后悔什么？”我说：“好吧，十年后，我可能仍然住在巴哈。我应该学习西班牙语，我应该学习如何冲浪，因为我们就在冲浪胜地旁边。” (01:02:29)：我做到了。我相信预期的后悔是一种智慧，它是采取行动的催化剂。这是一个数据点。另一个数据点是所谓的幸福 U 曲线，它已经存在了 20 年，它显示了以下内容。过去几年情况发生了变化，因为年轻人前所未有地不快乐。 20岁、22岁，真的不快乐，24岁，真的不快乐。 (01:02:58)：从历史上看，你从 18 岁到 23 岁或 24 岁都很快乐，然后在 23 岁或 24 岁左右，你开始看到生活满意度长期缓慢下降，实际上在 45 岁到 50 岁之间触底。我很遗憾地告诉你，莱尼，因为你已经 44 岁了，但你的里程可能会有所不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're saying I'm the least happy I'll ever be. That's only upside. That's great. Yeah.
turns.zh: 你说我是我这辈子最不快乐的人。这只是好处。那太棒了。是的。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Well, here's the part that's weird is that before this research was done, and it's global research across all demographics, what they found was starting around age 50 or 52, you get happier, so that you're happier in your fifties than your forties, sixties, fifties, seventies, happier than sixties, and the women in their eighties, happier than seventies. Wow. It's partly because we are in around 45 to 50, doing this thing called the midlife unraveling, what Brené Brown calls the midlife unraveling. (01:03:55): You're unraveling your expectations, what you define as success, your definition of what a beautiful body looks like, and you're liberated into freedom in your fifties and beyond. I can say that, yeah, I'm happier today at 64 than I was at 47 when I was going through my flatline experience, and not wanting to run my company anymore.
turns.zh: 嗯，奇怪的是，在这项研究完成之前，这是针对所有人口统计数据的全球研究，他们发现从 50 岁或 52 岁左右开始，你会变得更快乐，所以你在 50 岁时比 40 岁、60 岁、50 岁、70 岁更快乐，比 60 岁更快乐，而 80 岁的女性比 70 岁更快乐。哇。部分原因是我们在 45 岁到 50 岁左右，正在经历所谓的“中年解体”，Brené Brown 称之为“中年解体”。 (01:03:55)：你正在解开你的期望，你对成功的定义，你对美丽身体的定义，并且你在五十多岁时获得了自由。我可以说，是的，我今天 64 岁比 47 岁时更快乐，当时我正在经历平淡的经历，并且不想再经营我的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You used this term earlier, the midlife chrysalis, was that what it was?
turns.zh: 你之前用过这个词，中年蛹，是这个意思吗？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Chrysalis. Chrysalis, yeah.
turns.zh: 蛹。蛹，是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Chrysalis. What is that? Is that kind of along the same lines?
turns.zh: 蛹。那是什么？这是同样的路线吗？

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: If you think about the caterpillar to butterfly journey, midlife is the chrysalis. It's that cocoon in which all of the change is happening. At the time, when you're going through it, it's like, "Oh, shit. My life is liquefying in front of myself." On the other side of it, there's a metamorphosis that happens. (01:04:48): I like to use the language, in fact, I have a podcast called The Midlife Chrysalis, because I want to help change the dialogue around midlife, so that the number one word attached to midlife is not crisis, but in fact, it's maybe chrysalis, and the idea that life is meant to be transformative during that era.
turns.zh: 如果你想想毛毛虫到蝴蝶的旅程，中年就是蛹。所有的变化都在这个茧中发生。当时，当你经历它时，就像是，“哦，该死。我的生活在我自己面前液化了。”另一方面，发生了转变。 (01:04:48): 我喜欢用这种语言，事实上，我有一个播客叫《中年蛹》，因为我想帮助改变中年的对话，让中年的第一个词不是危机，但事实上，它可能是蛹，以及那个时代的生活意味着变革的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is actually very empowering. I am sort of going through that, not necessarily in this intense way yet, but that might be coming. You said there's a bunch of upsides to getting older. It might be helpful just to share a couple of those things for folks that are like, "Oh, wow, I didn't realize that."
turns.zh: 这实际上是非常有力量的。我正在经历这个过程，虽然还不一定是以这种激烈的方式，但那可能会到来。你说变老有很多好处。对于那些“哦，哇，我没有意识到这一点”的人来说，分享一些这样的事情可能会有所帮助。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Emotional intelligence grows with age. Our wisdom can grow with age, although we know 70-year-olds who are not as wise as 30-year-olds, so it's a matter of what you do with your life experience. I define wisdom as metabolized experience, mindfully shared for the common good. What else gets better with age? You learn how to edit. You have no more Fs left to give, no more fucks left to give. That is absolutely true, especially for women as they age. You are more spiritually curious. The list is long, and so there are a lot of things that, actually, another one that I love is you're not compartmentalized. (01:06:01): When you're younger, you're compartmentalized. As you grow older, you are growing whole, and that means you're alchemizing curiosity and wisdom, introvert, extrovert, masculine, feminine, gravitas, depth, and levity, lightness. The people who I really admire who are 85 years old, they're so present and they're so whole. They are just who they are.
turns.zh: 情商随着年龄的增长而增长。我们的智慧会随着年龄的增长而增长，尽管我们知道70岁的人不如30岁的人聪明，所以这取决于你如何利用你的生活经历。我将智慧定义为新陈代谢的经验，为了共同利益而用心分享。随着年龄的增长，还有什么会变得更好？您将学习如何编辑。你已经没有更多的Fs可以给予，没有更多的操蛋可以给予。这绝对是事实，尤其是对于上了年纪的女性来说。你在精神上更加好奇。这个清单很长，所以有很多事情，实际上，我喜欢的另一件事是你没有被划分。 (01:06:01)：当你年轻的时候，你会被划分。随着年龄的增长，你正在变得完整，这意味着你正在炼金术般的好奇心和智慧、内向、外向、男性、女性、庄严、深度、轻浮、轻松。我真正敬佩的那些85岁高龄的人，他们是如此的活在当下，他们是如此的完整。他们就是他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a quote I found from you along these lines, the societal narrative on aging is just don't do it.
turns.zh: 我从你那里找到了一句话，关于衰老的社会叙事是不要这样做。

turns.speaker: Chip Conley
turns.en: Fantastic. Yeah. We sort of say we don't want to age, but we do want to live. Quite frankly, aging and living are the same thing, as are aging and growing.
turns.zh: 极好的。是的。我们常说我们不想变老，但我们确实想活下去。坦率地说，衰老和生活是同一回事，衰老和成长也是同一回事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to MEA, just for folks that are interested, curious about this, who's this for, would you say? Who should seriously look into this program?
turns.zh: 回到MEA，只是为了那些对此感兴趣、好奇的人，你会说这是给谁的？谁应该认真研究这个计划？

Average age is 54, and it's people of all walks of life. It's not just the tech industry, but it's very popular in the tech industry. It's people who are looking to maybe do a reframe of their purpose, and maybe even a reinvention of their career. (01:07:29): Yeah, the two campuses are just gorgeous. It's been called the Four Seasons meets Blue Zones meets the Esalen Institute, which I like. We have online programs too, and so you don't have to come to either of our campuses in Mexico, or on the beach, or in New Mexico. You can actually do it online.
turns.zh: MEA 确实是，那些倾向于来到 MEA 的人正处于转型之中。可能是出售公司、辞职、离婚、生孩子、成为空巢老人、照顾父母直到他们去世、进行可怕的健康诊断。平均年龄54岁，来自各行各业。这不仅是科技行业，而且在科技行业非常受欢迎。这些人可能正在寻求重新构建自己的目标，甚至可能重塑自己的职业生涯。 (01:07:29)：是的，两个校区都很漂亮。它被称为“四个季节遇上蓝色区域遇上伊莎伦学院”，我喜欢这个。我们也有在线课程，因此您不必来到我们在墨西哥、海滩或新墨西哥州的任何一个校区。您实际上可以在线完成。

turns.en: The Four Seasons.

turns.en: Yeah, I have a daily blog. It's called Wisdom Well, and it's on the MEA website. When I'm looking for inspiration, AI does it for me, and ultimately, it gives me a first draft. That's good enough for me then to say, "Okay." There's times when I'm missing the inspiration. I tend to write really well in the morning. (01:08:47): If it's any other time of the day, I do not like writing creatively. If I have a deadline for tomorrow and it's five o'clock in the afternoon, it's like, "Okay, ChatGPT. I'm on my way to you." I tend to use ChatGPT the most because I don't know, I like Claude as well, but yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，我有一个每日博客。它被称为 Wisdom Well，位于 MEA 网站上。当我寻找灵感时，人工智能会为我做这件事，最终，它会给我一份初稿。这足以让我说：“好吧。”有时我会失去灵感。我倾向于早上写得很好。 (01:08:47)：如果是一天中的任何其他时间，我不喜欢创造性地写作。如果我明天有截止日期，而且是下午五点，我就会说：“好的，ChatGPT。我正在去见你的路上。”我最倾向于使用 ChatGPT，因为我不知道，我也喜欢 Claude，但是是的。

turns.zh: 好吧，太棒了。我想问一下你用的是什么工具。你在那里的工作流程是什么？你用的是语音模式吗？您是否只是输入“这就是我的想法，请给我写一篇简短的博客文章？”
